```{r libraries, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Load tidyverse, which includes the packages: ggplot2 (a package for plots) and
# dplyr (a package for wrangling data)
library(tidyverse)
# load broom which is a package that prints tables neatly 
# we'll use it to print regression tables
library(broom)
# load ggrepel, which is a package to print text on a graph neatly
# we'll use it later when making scatterplots
library(ggrepel)

# Load data: the `../` bit means "go to the folder one level above the folder in which this script is saved"
load("../data/jobs.RData")

```

## Recap from Tutorial 4

Let's plot the scatterplot with line fit corresponding to the equation:
$$Wage_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Education_i + \beta_2MediumIncome_i + \beta_3HighIncome_i + \varepsilon_i.$$

```{r wage-educ-income-scatter-1}

# Regression with common slope and different intercepts
wage_educ_income_reg <- lm(
  median_wage_rate ~ avg_years_of_education +
    medium_income_occ + high_income_occ,
  data = jobs
)

tidy(wage_educ_income_reg)

# Store coefficients
educ_slope <- coef(wage_educ_income_reg)["avg_years_of_education"]

low_intercept <- coef(wage_educ_income_reg)["(Intercept)"]

medium_intercept <- coef(wage_educ_income_reg)["(Intercept)"] +
  coef(wage_educ_income_reg)["medium_income_occ"]

high_intercept <- coef(wage_educ_income_reg)["(Intercept)"] +
  coef(wage_educ_income_reg)["high_income_occ"]


# Plot
ggplot(jobs, aes(x = avg_years_of_education,
                 y = median_wage_rate)) +
  
  # Scatter points
  geom_point(data = subset(jobs, low_income_occ == 1),
             aes(colour = "Low")) +
  geom_point(data = subset(jobs, medium_income_occ == 1),
             aes(colour = "Medium")) +
  geom_point(data = subset(jobs, high_income_occ == 1),
             aes(colour = "High")) +
  
  # Parallel fitted lines
  geom_abline(aes(intercept = low_intercept,
                  slope = educ_slope,
                  colour = "Low"),
              linewidth = 1) +
  
  geom_abline(aes(intercept = medium_intercept,
                  slope = educ_slope,
                  colour = "Medium"),
              linewidth = 1) +
  
  geom_abline(aes(intercept = high_intercept,
                  slope = educ_slope,
                  colour = "High"),
              linewidth = 1) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Wage Rate vs Education by Income Level",
    x = "Average Years of Education",
    y = "Median Wage Rate",
    colour = "Income Level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


In the figure drawn below, note the mean education, and mean wage for each of the 3 occupation groups in the dotted lines.
```{r wage-educ-inclines-scatter}
# Group means
low_mean_wage <- mean(
  jobs$median_wage_rate[jobs$low_income_occ == 1],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
low_mean_educ <- mean(
  jobs$avg_years_of_education[jobs$low_income_occ == 1],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

medium_mean_wage <- mean(
  jobs$median_wage_rate[jobs$medium_income_occ == 1],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
medium_mean_educ <- mean(
  jobs$avg_years_of_education[jobs$medium_income_occ == 1],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

high_mean_wage <- mean(
  jobs$median_wage_rate[jobs$high_income_occ == 1],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
high_mean_educ <- mean(
  jobs$avg_years_of_education[jobs$high_income_occ == 1],
  na.rm = TRUE
)


# Plot
ggplot(jobs, aes(x = avg_years_of_education,
                 y = median_wage_rate)) +
  
  # Scatter points
  geom_point(
    data = subset(jobs, low_income_occ == 1),
    aes(colour = "Low")
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(jobs, medium_income_occ == 1),
    aes(colour = "Medium")
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(jobs, high_income_occ == 1),
    aes(colour = "High")
  ) +
  
  # Mean education: vertical lines
  geom_vline(
    aes(xintercept = low_mean_educ, colour = "Low"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    aes(xintercept = medium_mean_educ, colour = "Medium"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    aes(xintercept = high_mean_educ, colour = "High"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  
  # Mean wage: horizontal lines
  geom_hline(
    aes(yintercept = low_mean_wage, colour = "Low"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    aes(yintercept = medium_mean_wage, colour = "Medium"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    aes(yintercept = high_mean_wage, colour = "High"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Wage Rate vs Education by Income Level",
    x = "Average Years of Education",
    y = "Median Wage Rate",
    colour = "Income Level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

We are going to now show that the interpreting the relationship between education and wage given by $\beta_1$ in the equation below, has a similar logic as the de-meaning step simple linear regression model from Lecture 1 and Tutorial 2. 

$$Wage_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Education_i + \beta_2MediumIncome_i + \beta_3HighIncome_i + \varepsilon_i.$$

The only difference here is that we do this now for each income group separately.

Let us de-mean the scattered points for each occupation group by its average education and wage rate shown by the dotted lines. 

(We can de-mean the variables by taking the residuals as shown below. For a step-by-step explanation of why the residuals give the de-meaned version, see the code solutions to Tutorial 4.)

After de-meaning, we plot the scatterplot of the wage and education groups with a line and a confidence interval for the line.

```{r residual-regressions}

# (1) Regress wage rate on the three income-level dummies
reg_wage <- lm(
  median_wage_rate ~ low_income_occ + medium_income_occ + high_income_occ - 1,
  data = jobs
)

# (2) Regress education on the three income-level dummies
reg_education <- lm(
  avg_years_of_education ~ low_income_occ + medium_income_occ + high_income_occ - 1,
  data = jobs
)

# Store residuals as new columns
jobs$wage_residual <- residuals(reg_wage)
jobs$education_residual <- residuals(reg_education)


# Plot residualised wage against residualised education
ggplot(jobs, aes(x = education_residual,
                 y = wage_residual)) +
  
  geom_point(data = subset(jobs, low_income_occ == 1),
             aes(colour = "Low")) +
  
  geom_point(data = subset(jobs, medium_income_occ == 1),
             aes(colour = "Medium")) +
  
  geom_point(data = subset(jobs, high_income_occ == 1),
             aes(colour = "High")) +
  
  # Linear fit with 95% confidence interval
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = TRUE,
    colour = "black",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 6)
  ) +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 6)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Wage Rate vs Education",
    subtitle = "Controlling for Income Level",
    x = "Average Years of Education (after accounting for income level)",
    y = "Median Wage Rate (after accounting for income level)",
    colour = "Income Level"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()

```
We wanted to show that the slope of this regression where wage and education are de-meaned by the group averages are the exact same as $\beta_1$ from the regression: 
$$Wage_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Education_i + \beta_2MediumIncome_i + \beta_3HighIncome_i + \varepsilon_i.$$

Let's run the 2 regressions and compare the coefficient for the education and education residual variable --- it would be the exact same. The standard errors are the same when rounded up to 2 decimal places (they're off by a few decimal points for a technical reason that's beyond the scope of this course).

```{r verify-2-regressions}

model1 <- lm(wage_residual ~ education_residual, data = jobs)
tidy(model1)

model2 <- lm(
  median_wage_rate ~ avg_years_of_education +
    medium_income_occ + high_income_occ,
  data = jobs
)

tidy(model2)
```

If you want to focus on a particular x-y relationship like wage and education above, adding more dummy variables as regressors is basically de-meaning the main outcome and regressor of interest by the dummy variables. 

A similar interpretation also applies to other multiple linear regression models. If you add continuous variables or interactions (as you saw in Lecture 2 with Simon), it's technically a little more involved but the idea is the same --- all other regressors (or controls) remove their average influence on the main x and y of interest. The R script in Tutorial 4 has one such example of this.

This interpretation will become useful when you come to Panel data and Difference-in-Difference models.


## Tutorial 5, 1.5: Choosing a model

First we select the training sample
```{r select-train-sample}

# Set seed so the same sample is drawn each time
set.seed(123)

# Draw 300 SOC codes, excluding 2211 and 2212
sample_soc_codes <- jobs %>%
  filter(!soc_code %in% c(2211, 2212)) %>%
  distinct(soc_code) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 300) %>%
  pull(soc_code)

# Create estimation sample
estimation_sample <- jobs %>%
  filter(soc_code %in% sample_soc_codes)
```

Then we select the test sample
```{r select-holdout-sample}
# Create holdout sample
holdout_sample <- jobs %>%
  filter(
    !soc_code %in% sample_soc_codes
  )

```


Here's a model that I'm going to use for OLS. This code will give you an error. You have to make exactly 1 modification to make the code run. Modify and run the code:
```{r ols-train}
# Estimate pre-defined model by running an ols regression
ols_train_model <- (
  median_wage_rate ~ avg_years_of_education +
    medium_income_occ + high_income_occ +
    weighted_skill_score +
    number_of_transferable_skills +
    years_of_experience +
    I(years_of_experience^2),
  data = estimation_sample
)

# Regression results
tidy(ols_train_model)

```


Here, I'm going to train a LASSO model. The details of this code is not important to you. The only thing you need to know is what the model is taking as input. Look at the `select()` function in `x_train`, and then look at `y_train`. What variables have I asked the model to choose from? Have I omitted some variables?

```{r lasso-train}
library(glmnet)

# Create predictor matrix using training sample
x_train <- estimation_sample %>%
  select(
    -median_wage_rate,
    -soc_code,
    -soc_description,
    -median_hours_worked,
    -wage_residual,
    -education_residual
  ) %>%
  model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = .)

# Outcome
y_train <- estimation_sample$median_wage_rate

# Cross-validated LASSO
set.seed(123)

lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(
  x = x_train,
  y = y_train,
  alpha = 1
)

# Extract coefficients at the optimal lambda
lasso_coefs <- coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.min")

# Keep only variables selected by LASSO
selected_model <- data.frame(
  variable = rownames(lasso_coefs),
  coefficient = as.numeric(lasso_coefs)
) %>%
  filter(coefficient != 0)

# Print selected model
print(selected_model)
```

## Tutorial 5, 1.6: Out-of-sample predictions

Now we compare the predictions generated by the estimated OLS model from above with the actual values from the holdout or test sample.

The code below is supposed to make a scatterplot, but it won't work. You'll have to make exactly 1 slight modification to make it work.

```{r ols-test}
# Generate predictions using the model estimated on the training sample
holdout_sample <- holdout_sample %>%
  mutate(
    ols_predicted_wage = predict(
      ols_train_model,
      newdata = holdout_sample
    )
  )

# Plot predicted against true wage
ggplot(
  holdout_sample,
  aes(
    x = ols_predicted_wage,
    y = median_wage_rate
  )
) +
  geom_(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  
  
  geom_text_repel(
    data = subset(holdout_sample, soc_code %in% c(2211, 2212)),
    aes(label = soc_description),
    size = 4,
    max.overlaps = Inf
  ) +
  
  # 45-degree line: perfect prediction
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "True Wage Rate vs OLS Predicted Wage Rate",
    subtitle = "Holdout Sample",
    x = "OLS Predicted Median Wage Rate",
    y = "True Median Wage Rate"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```

How well did the OLS model perform? How did it perform specifically for the average worker in the 2 job categories for doctors?

The below code will work, try it.

```{r lasso-test}
# Create predictor matrix for holdout sample
x_holdout <- holdout_sample %>%
  select(
    -median_wage_rate,
    -soc_code,
    -soc_description,
    -median_hours_worked,
    -wage_residual,
    -education_residual,
    -ols_predicted_wage
  ) %>%
  model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = .)

# Match training columns and their order
x_holdout <- x_holdout[, colnames(x_train), drop = FALSE]

# Generate LASSO predictions
holdout_sample <- holdout_sample %>%
  mutate(
    lasso_predicted_wage = as.numeric(
      predict(
        lasso_cv,
        newx = x_holdout,
        s = "lambda.min"
      )
    )
  )


# Plot predicted against actual wage with lasso predictions
ggplot(
  holdout_sample,
  aes(
    x = lasso_predicted_wage,
    y = median_wage_rate
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  
  # Label SOC codes 2211 and 2212
  geom_text_repel(
    data = subset(holdout_sample, soc_code %in% c(2211, 2212)),
    aes(label = soc_description),
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  # 45-degree line: perfect prediction
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "True Wage Rate vs LASSO Predicted",
    subtitle = "Holdout Sample with SOC 2211 and 2212 Labelled",
    x = "LASSO Predicted Median Wage Rate",
    y = "True Median Wage Rate"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```

How well did the LASSO model perform? How did it perform specifically for the average worker in the 2 job categories for doctors?


The $R^2$ can be (but doesn't need to be) a measure of model performance. A value closer to 1 is generally seen as being better. For reasons (unfortunately, because I would love to go on about it) beyond the scope of this module, the $R^2$ below is actually pretty good for this case study.

```{r}
summary(lm(median_wage_rate ~ lasso_predicted_wage, data = holdout_sample))$r.squared
summary(lm(median_wage_rate ~ ols_predicted_wage, data = holdout_sample))$r.squared
```

We can also compare OLS and LASSO predictions. Based on the analysis so far, which model would you select and why?
```{r}
# Compare OLS and LASSO predictions
ggplot(
  holdout_sample,
  aes(
    x = ols_predicted_wage,
    y = lasso_predicted_wage
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  
  # Label SOC codes 2211 and 2212
  geom_text_repel(
    data = subset(holdout_sample, soc_code %in% c(2211, 2212)),
    aes(label = soc_description),
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  # 45-degree line: models make same prediction
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "OLS vs LASSO Wage Predictions",
    subtitle = "Holdout Sample with SOC 2211 and 2212 Labelled",
    x = "OLS Predicted Median Wage Rate",
    y = "LASSO Predicted Median Wage Rate"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```
